title: Disney+ to stream upcoming Super Bowl
content: Disney announced Wednesday that its streaming service Disney+ will air the upcoming Super Bowl in February. The 2027 championship game, as well as two Monday Night Football games leading up to the Super Bowl, will be available to all Disney+ subscribers in the U.S. Disney had previously announced that its ESPN sports division would produce the Super Bowl in 2027 for the first time ever. The game will air on ESPN and Disney's broadcast network, ABC. Interest in the upcoming Super Bowl is already high. Disney said on its most recent earnings call that ad spots for the game are already sold out, the earliest sellout in Super Bowl history, according to a press release. The announcement is the latest move in Disney's efforts to expand its live sports streaming offerings. The media company last year launched a standalone ESPN streaming service , bringing the content outside the cable bundle. In August, Disney announced that Formula E — the open-wheel racing championship for electric cars — will be available to Disney+ subscribers beginning Dec. 18. Other streamers are also using live sports to bolster their portfolios. CNBC reported last week that Alphabet's YouTube is actively searching for additional live sports rights. YouTube already pays roughly $2 billion annually for the rights to "NFL Sunday Ticket," which will last until the end of the 2029-30 season. Netflix will air five NFL games during the 2026-27 season. Netflix Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria said in a CNBC interview last month that the company would be open to acquiring the rights to international NFL games if they become available.

title: Suffragette role 'a gift' says Beverley Knight
content:
Singer Beverley Knight said she hoped audiences watching her latest musical would leave feeling "empowered" and with the belief that their voices can make a difference.
Sylvia the Musical tells the story of suffragette Sylvia Pankhurst and the family rift caused by the fight for women's voting rights.
The Wolverhampton artist, who plays Sylvia's mother and suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst at the Birmingham Hippodrome said she was a "history nerd" and described the part as a "gift of a role".
"It's an absolutely killer story, and the best thing is it's true," she said.
"I want everyone bouncing out of there because it's a joyful musical, even though there's some absolutely heartbreaking moments in it."
The soul singer, known for hits including Shoulda Woulda Coulda and Get Up, told BBC Radio WM the musical was telling a "huge part of British history" from 1903, all the way to 1928.
"So most people know who Emmeline Pankhurst was, leader of the suffragettes, she was determined to get women the vote," she explained.
"But she came up against her middle daughter Sylvia, who not only wanted to get wealthy property owning women the vote, which was the case with men in the country, [you] had to be rich and male to vote, she wanted everybody to be able to vote.
"But Emmeline was focused on just the women and that put her on a collision course with her daughter and both of them were on a collision course with the government."
Knight added the show, which also features Naomi Katiyo as Sylvia Pankhurst, was "musically up my street" and was being called a "hip-hop musical" because it included elements of R&B, funk, soul, garage, gospel and house.
"The engine of the show is the music," she said. The whole thing is either spoken or rapped or sung. Of course, I'm doing mostly singing because I ain't rapping anything."
The former Highfields School pupil explained the story also went beyond the Pankhurst family, with some people who attended the show likely to have relatives who were involved in the suffragette movement.
"It's not just the story of the Pankhursts, there are going to be loads of people who will come to this show who will be like... my grandma or my great-grandma, she was involved in the suffragette movement.
"I want everybody to leave like, let's go, oh my god, that feeling of I can effect change, I can use my voice and effect change. I feel empowered."

title: How boxing inspired a play about men's mental health
content:
For many athletes, years of training can provide a routine, a purpose and an identity - but what happens when it all stops?
That question is at the heart of a new play which explores men's mental health through the world of boxing.
The Corner Man follows a fighter forced to confront life outside the ring after spending years dedicated to the sport.
Through his story, the play explores losing a sense of purpose, the difficulty some men have talking about their mental health and the support they can find in each other.
Writer and producer Cathal J Ferris said the idea grew from his own experience of boxing and conversations with fighters.
"What is a boxer after he retires really played on my mind," he said, adding that the same questions around identity and purpose can apply beyond sport.
The play follows Liam Casey, who has dedicated much of his life to boxing, from the age of about nine into his 30s.
For Ferris, the story is not only about leaving the ring, but about losing the routine that comes with it.
"The idea of structure and what life is like whenever you lose that structure definitely played on my mind," he said.
"There are people who work in jobs for 10, 12, 13-odd years and just decide to change industries.
"I think there's a lot of people who may not know what to do with themselves after."
Ferris grew up performing in amateur theatre in Belfast and Lisburn before going to drama school in London in 2012.
He said returning home had given him the chance to tell new stories about the place where he grew up.
"I'm a Belfast boy at heart, and it is great to tell stories from the city," he said.
Ferris said "the boxing community in Belfast is phenomenal" and that it played an important part in shaping the story.
Alongside boxing, the play also looks at how men talk - or sometimes do not talk - about their mental health.
"I think the old phrase is 'say nothing', and we know that all too well," Ferris said.
"As a man, it is definitely hard for myself to talk about these things, and I try to be a little bit more open."
In the play, Liam struggles with life after boxing, but it is the other men around him who help provide a support network - something Ferris said was an important part of the story.
"It is healthy to talk, so definitely if you're a man and you're struggling, at least speak to somebody," he said.

title: The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆
content:
This sequel to The Social Network dramatises how a Facebook whistleblower exposed the company's secrets. But with a "dead-eyed" Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg, it lacks thrills.
It may be a film about a bunch of nerds setting up a website, but The Social Network (2010) won three Oscars and was nominated for five more. Directed by David Fincher, scripted by Aaron Sorkin, and starring Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg, it somehow made Facebook's teething problems as dazzlingly entertaining as any stunt-packed spy caper. Sixteen years on, we have The Social Reckoning, a sort-of sequel which had the potential to be even more exciting.
Once again, its focus is Facebook, but this time Sorkin is the director as well as the screenwriter, and Jeremy Strong from Succession has taken over the role of Zuckerberg. While Eisenberg played him as a petulant princeling, Strong's version, like so many of his characters, is a dead-eyed, unsmiling boss from hell.
There are other changes, too. The Social Network dramatised the legal squabbles between the Harvard students behind Facebook, whereas The Social Reckoning has a whistleblower and a journalist exposing the damage done to the world by social media. In a way, then, it tells a much bigger story than its predecessor. But in every way that counts, it's a much smaller film. Ironically, Sorkin's main theme is the alarming power that social media platforms have to influence us, but The Social Reckoning itself is unlikely to influence anyone.
Jeremy Allen White stars as Jeff Horwitz, an investigative reporter who transfers to the Wall Street Journal's San Francisco office in 2019. He wants to find out what's going at Facebook, but none of its staff will talk to him until he contacts Frances Haugen, played by Mikey Madison, the Oscar-winning star of Anora . At a secret meeting, Haugen tells him that users are being pushed towards extremist groups – and that's just one of the issues she has uncovered while working in the company's Civic Integrity team.
So far, so promising: Sorkin is aiming at a crusading newspaper drama in the tradition of All the President's Men and Spotlight, and at times he almost hits the target. The opening sequence is a queasily credible portrait of someone who has been radicalised online, and the facts and figures about Facebook's impact on mental health are sobering: Horwitz learns that, according to internal research kept secret by the Facebook-owned Instagram , 32% of teenage girls with body-related anxieties felt worse after using it.
But The Social Reckoning doesn't have the tension or the urgency that such films need – or indeed the dynamism that Fincher might have brought to the project. No one ever threatens Horwitz or Haugen. They keep saying that they could be in danger, but they never actually are.
Unlike in The Social Network, Zuckerberg is a minor character with no inner life. Madison has a fraction of the ferocious energy she had in Anora. (Haugen, incidentally, is blue-eyed and blonde-haired, and was in her late-30s when the story took place, so Madison couldn't look less her if she tried.) And while Horvitz won a Pulitzer Prize for his articles, in the film his sleuthing amounts to talking to Haugen and setting up a fake Facebook account. Even more disappointingly, he is never seen in the headband he wore for one memorable TV news appearance.
The Social Reckoning
Director: Aaron Sorkin
Cast: Jeremy Strong, Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White
Run-time: 1hr 52m
Release date: 9 October in US and UK cinemas
Sorkin tries to add some momentum to his uneventful narrative by flipping back and forth between two timelines. In one of these, Horwitz and Haugen have their chats, all of which consist of her handing him some information, claiming that she loves her job, and insisting that she won't help him again (spoiler alert: she will). In the other strand, Zuckerberg rehearses for a senate hearing. Sorkin raises a few smiles with his trademark perky, quirky banter, as Zuckerberg's advisers instruct him on how to appear less robotic when giving his testimony, and Haugen chides Horwitz about his lack of tech knowledge (his one and only character trait). But neither of these repetitive strands has any real conflict. And, inconveniently for Sorkin, they never intertwine: Zuckerberg doesn't have any interaction with Horwitz or Haugen.
One of the film's fundamental problems is that Facebook is still going strong, and Zuckerberg is still worth more than $200 billion, so the viewer knows all along that there isn't an All The President's Men-style giant-killing finale in store. Despite its fire-and-brimstone title, in other words, The Social Reckoning doesn't have much of a reckoning.
But the main problem is that the drab drama just isn't intense enough to change anyone's mind. It's part of a current wave of films about super-rich industrialists that includes Alejandro G Iñárritu gonzo Tom Cruise vehicle, Digger , Alex Gibney's provocative Elon Musk documentary, Musk , and Luca Guadagnino's stylish biopic of Sam Altman, Artificial. But Sorkin's effort is the mildest and least ambitious of the bunch. You would probably keep watching if you caught it on television, but you might well scroll through your social media feed at the same time.
★★☆☆☆

title: King Charles and Elton John in the audience for Apple music workshop
content:
King Charles has visited a hi-tech music workshop for young people, in a collaboration between his King's Trust charity and technology firm Apple.
Pop royalty, in the form of Sir Elton John, was a special guest at the event, sitting beside the King, as they listened to a short performance from singer-songwriter Skye Newman.
The event was held at a music hall in Apple's headquarters building, in the restored Battersea Power Station in south west London.
The project being backed by the King is intended to equip young people with practical skills to work in the creative industries.
The King was introduced to Prophet Guillory, Apple Music's head of artist services, tools and community, who was praised for his work as a mentor for young people.
"Wow, you did your homework," Prophet said, when the King seemed familiar with his efforts.
The King was introduced to young performers at the event.
Another young musician said the problem was getting the money together to launch creative ideas.
Young performer Skye Newman faced what must have seemed like a very unusual X-Factor style panel - King Charles, Sir Elton, his husband David Furnish and Apple's executive chairman Tim Cook.
The music workshop was part of a project between Apple and the King's Trust Creative Labs, and is the latest link-up between the royals and the Californian tech giant.
Last year, the King revealed a playlist of 17 of his favourite tracks , which was issued on Apple Music.
The King didn't include Sir Elton John in any of those choices - but the pop star has been a long-time supporter of the King's Trust charity, which was previously known as the Prince's Trust.
Now in its 50th year , the charity was set up to give opportunities to deprived and marginalised young people - and has so far helped 1.3 million people across the UK.
The tie-up with Apple shows the changing demands for work skills, including using the latest technology for young people wanting to build careers in the music and creative industries.
There was also a royal link with Battersea Power Station - as that had once provided the electricity for Buckingham Palace.
In the power station's control room, the link to the Palace had been discreetly labelled as "Carnaby Street", in case any intruders had ever been tempted to switch off the Palace lights.

title: Gavin and Stacey creators Jones and Corden reveal celebrity cast of new show
content:
Gavin and Stacey co-creators Ruth Jones and James Corden have revealed details about their new TV comedy drama series The Choir.
The eight-episode show will air on Apple TV and feature guest appearances by Ted Lasso's Hannah Waddingham, X-Men's James McAvoy and Harry Potter's Jim Broadbent.
The series follows brother Ben (Corden) and sister Lisa (Jones), who have not seen each other for several years.
The pair previously said the idea came from their family connection to choirs , with Corden's mum and Jones' sister both members of one.
Ben has been living abroad, while Lisa has continued living in their small town where "nothing ever happens".
But when events take a sorry turn, Ben is forced to return to "a life he never wanted, a town he never liked and a family from which he's estranged".
The cast includes Tom Davis, Rosie Sheehy, Susan Brown, Jason Watkins, Alexandira Riley, Sylvestra Le Touzel, Tom Edden, Gary Lamont, Emily Lloyd-Saini, Stephen Leask, Luiis Rouf, Jo Foster, Evie Jones and Farrah Abbassy.
Jones and Corden are executive producers for the series, which is now in production and set to air in 2027.
Jones previously said: "We both feel that choirs, amateur choirs especially, bring people together in a way that maybe nothing else does.
"There was just this idea to bring this group of characters together from different backgrounds, all sorts of different things going on in their lives."
Corden added they wanted "to try and make a show about community and the importance of community".
"It's just about a group of people that come together every week and enjoy and sing, and it's really about the life that's within that," he added.
When Jones and Corden first met in 2000, they never imagined it would lead to 22 episodes of a record-breaking TV show.
The pair were filming Fat Friends at the Crowne Plaza in Leeds and formed an unexpected friendship.
They then co-wrote Gavin and Stacey, in which they played Vanessa "Nessa" Jenkins and Neil "Smithy" Smith, the best friends of the title characters
The hit comedy ran for three series, and three Christmas specials, between 2007 and 2024.
Their memoir was published on 9 October - almost a year on from the show's record-breaking finale on Christmas Day 2024.
Alongside their new collaboration, Jones recently appeared in new Netflix series Run Away - based on the Harlan Coben novel.
She has also teamed up with Steve Speirs in a six-part comedy series called Better Later, about the challenges of relationships in middle age.
Jones recently portrayed Mrs Bennet in another comedy series, The Other Bennet Sister, which was inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, while Corden has just finished a stint on Broadway.

title: Xbox bets on Gears of War in battle of gaming giants
content:
Gears of War, one of the video games that helped Microsoft's Xbox to win over millions of fans, is back.
Prequel E-Day takes players back to where it all started, telling the origin story of humanity's conflict with The Locust - the series' horrifying enemy species.
The game's been well-received by critics and players, but it's also seen as a big test of Xbox's new direction.
Unlike recent flagship titles from the company's studios, which have been released on PlayStation 5 and, in some cases, Nintendo Switch, E-Day is being pushed as an Xbox exclusive.
The apparent goal is to draw players back to the brand, but critics have questioned whether that's realistic at a time when console prices are higher than ever .
BBC Newsbeat spoke to developer The Coalition - the makers of E-Day - about what staying exclusive means to them.
Gears of War has been one of Xbox's flagship series since it launched back in 2006.
Creative director Matt Searcy tells Newsbeat the sci-fi shooter is a "mix of war story with comic book-y monsters that come out of the ground".
"It's a video game with a lot of heart, a lot of blood and guts," he says.
First released on the Xbox 360, Gears helped to popularise "cover-shooter" gameplay, which encouraged players to shelter from enemy attacks.
It brought a strategic dimension to third-person action games, and also won fans with its co-operative multiplayer modes - a feature that's returned for E-Day.
But, 20 years later, Xbox finds itself in a very different position in the console space.
It's seen as a third-place competitor, behind both Sony's PlayStation and Nintendo's Switch consoles.
Previous CEO Phil Spencer had begun to take the division in a new direction, releasing some of its most popular games on rival consoles for the first time.
E-Day was widely expected to follow other high budget series such as Halo on to other companies' machines.
But new Xbox boss Asha Sharma, who took over the job in February, announced Gears of War would remain a "console exclusive", although a PC version has also been released.
Her strategy has been called into question by critics.
After taking six years to make and an estimated budget in the hundreds of millions, they argue that keeping E-Day away from other platforms could mean it's less likely to make back its development cost.
Coalition studio head Mike Crump says E-Day is a "natural choice to be an exclusive".
"Gears has been an exclusive franchise to Xbox for 20 years now. It's sort of entwined deeply with the brand," he says.
